title: A CLOs Perspective on the AI Value Proposition
author: Mark A. Smolik

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Smolik does not engage the cluster’s central concern that AI may undermine junior-generated revenue, leverage and apprenticeship. Instead, he reframes AI primarily as augmentation that can improve professional value, with adoption led through experimentation, ethics and judgment. He anticipates changes in how legal services are bought and sold, but offers analogy and prediction rather than evidence about pyramid restructuring or training effects.
qs: ## The Age of the Augmented Lawyer  The lawyers and legal professionals who thrive in our hypercompetitive industry will be those who embrace augmentation — who see AI not as a threat or as competition, but as an opportunity to learn, improve and drive value.
It also means grounding the adoption of AI in ethics, judgment, and integrity — the timeless foundations of our profession.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Smolik accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will reshape legal-service delivery through augmentation, process integration and data-driven operating change. He materially extends its bargaining-power argument from a CLO perspective: AI-enabled invoice review, rate benchmarking, staffing analysis and workflow data could make legal departments stronger purchasers and pressure outside firms to deliver greater value at lower total cost. His adoption evidence remains qualitative and his broader effects are principally predictions.
qs: While there remains a great deal to learn about the impact and potential of AI in the legal industry, I believe it will significantly change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold.

It will also help evolve legal services into a data-rich product which will not only create new opportunities but also help law departments (as the purchaser of legal services) make better and more powerful buying decisions fueling a shift in the buy-sell dynamic.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Smolik directly supports the proposition that corporate legal departments can capture AI gains by integrating AI with structured data and core processes, improving internal productivity and strengthening purchasing decisions toward outside counsel. He also aligns with augmentation rather than replacement. His claims are mainly predictive and qualitative, however, and do not independently establish quantified savings or market-wide transformation.
qs: It will also help evolve legal services into a data-rich product which will not only create new opportunities but also help law departments (as the purchaser of legal services) make better and more powerful buying decisions fueling a shift in the buy-sell dynamic.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Smolik supports the cluster’s principal augmentation thesis: AI should automate routine legal work and expand professional capacity rather than replace lawyers. He also endorses leadership-driven experimentation grounded in ethics and judgment. His account is more optimistic and predictive than the synthesis, however, and does not substantively address verification burdens, uneven task performance or apprenticeship and competence risks.
qs: Used effectively, AI will (and is already) enabling legal professionals to deliver services cheaper, faster, and better — not by replacing us, but by augmenting us.
It also means grounding the adoption of AI in ethics, judgment, and integrity — the timeless foundations of our profession.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Smolik broadly supports the cluster’s restructuring thesis: he expects AI to significantly change legal-service delivery and markets while acknowledging uncertainty, and his historical analogy suggests technology can raise productivity without simply removing legal work. However, he provides no evidence or position on broad displacement or the specific risk to junior pipelines.
qs: While there remains a great deal to learn about the impact and potential of AI in the legal industry, I believe it will significantly change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold.
These changes enabled us to be more responsive and productive, but they also put considerably more demands on our time as speed to respond became the norm.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Smolik supports the cluster’s core view that AI can enhance lawyers’ work while materially reshaping legal-service delivery and commercial models. His historical analogy also reinforces that productivity gains may increase responsiveness demands rather than straightforwardly reduce workload, although he provides no direct evidence on staffing or employment effects.
qs: These changes enabled us to be more responsive and productive, but they also put considerably more demands on our time as speed to respond became the norm.
While there remains a great deal to learn about the impact and potential of AI in the legal industry, I believe it will significantly change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: Smolik supports the cluster’s proposition that AI-created value will depend on changes in legal delivery and buyer–provider relationships, not merely task efficiency. He particularly reinforces the buyer-power strand by predicting that data-rich services, workflow analysis and benchmarking will strengthen corporate legal departments’ purchasing decisions, while acknowledging uncertainty and offering no quantified market-wide results.
qs: While there remains a great deal to learn about the impact and potential of AI in the legal industry, I believe it will significantly change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold.

It will also help evolve legal services into a data-rich product which will not only create new opportunities but also help law departments (as the purchaser of legal services) make better and more powerful buying decisions fueling a shift in the buy-sell dynamic.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that AI should augment rather than replace legal professionals and that value depends on integrating it into organisational processes under human judgment and ethical leadership. Its claims are mostly prospective and do not materially address the cluster’s stronger cautions about jagged capability, task-specific testing or verification burdens.
qs: Used effectively, AI will (and is already) enabling legal professionals to deliver services cheaper, faster, and better — not by replacing us, but by augmenting us.

kp.k: Earlier technologies increased productivity but also responsiveness demands
kp.d: Reflecting on practice beginning in 1987, Smolik describes successive communications technologies as improving responsiveness and productivity while increasing demands on lawyers' time. He uses this historical experience as context for his view that AI represents a substantially greater change.
qs: These changes enabled us to be more responsive and productive, but they also put considerably more demands on our time as speed to respond became the norm.
They helped transform our profession — but nothing compares to what's happening now.

kp.k: AI could shift purchasing power toward law departments
kp.d: Smolik predicts that extracting information previously inaccessible in physical files will change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold. He expects automation of invoice review, rate benchmarking, staffing analysis and workflow evaluation to turn legal services into a data-rich product and strengthen corporate legal departments' buying decisions. He acknowledges that much remains to be learned about AI's impact and potential.
qs: While there remains a great deal to learn about the impact and potential of AI in the legal industry, I believe it will significantly change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold.

AI will give law departments the ability to automate repetitive tasks such as the review of invoices, benchmark rates, analyze staffing patterns, evaluate workflows, and identify risks and opportunities in ways that were previously not possible.

It will also help evolve legal services into a data-rich product which will not only create new opportunities but also help law departments (as the purchaser of legal services) make better and more powerful buying decisions fueling a shift in the buy-sell dynamic.

kp.k: Augmentation, rather than replacement, defines AI's value
kp.d: Smolik characterizes AI as a capability-enhancing resource rather than a tool. He reports that his DHL team is exploring its use to expand capacity and improve service at lower total cost, and describes similar efforts at Duracell, Cargill, Mars Wrigley and Coherent as achieving remarkable results. These are practitioner assertions without quantified outcomes in the article; his broader claim combines present benefits with predicted augmentation rather than replacement.
qs: It's a resource that enhances capabilities.

Among my team at DHL, we go to great lengths to leverage AI seeking new and creative ways to augment our capacity, enhance our service capabilities and lay the groundwork for delivering services better, faster and at a total lower cost.
Used effectively, AI will (and is already) enabling legal professionals to deliver services cheaper, faster, and better — not by replacing us, but by augmenting us.

kp.k: Structured data supports productivity and better legal decisions
kp.d: Smolik predicts that AI applied to structured data will automate repetitive work, improve information access, expand individual and team capacity, and enable quicker assessment of risks and opportunities. He argues that the ability to use data and AI will distinguish value-creating legal departments from those struggling with mounting cost pressure.
qs: Leveraging structured (organized) data, AI will significantly expand individual, team and organizational productivity.
It will help automate what's repetitive and enable "fingertip" access to information helping us better evaluate risks and opportunities and drive quicker and better decision making.
Those who do not will struggle particularly as the pressure on law department leaders to lower costs continues to build.

kp.k: Core-process integration promises quality, foresight and lower costs
kp.d: Smolik presents efficiency, consistency in high-volume work, predictive anticipation of problems, data-grounded decision-making and lower overall legal cost as opportunities from integrating AI into core departmental processes. These are prospective benefits, not measured findings. He argues that maximizing them also requires outside law firms to embrace the same approach with lower total service cost as an objective.
qs: By integrating AI into core processes, law departments will have the opportunity to:
Increase consistency and quality across high-volume work
Enable foresight, using predictive analytics to anticipate problems before they occur
Support better decision-making, grounded in real data not snippets of recalled experiences
But, in order to maximize that value the law firms we use need to also embrace these concepts with a view toward the delivery of services at a total lower cost.

kp.k: Routine-work automation could restore personal time
kp.d: Against a backdrop of heavy workloads, tight budgets, lean teams and high expectations, Smolik suggests that AI handling routine research, drafting and analysis could return time to legal professionals. He frames improved work-life balance as a possibility alongside greater productivity, rather than an established outcome.
qs: Budgets are tight, teams are lean, expectations are high, and work-life balance often feels out of reach.

By taking on the time-consuming task of routine and repetitive (commodity type) legal work — the research, the drafting, the analyzing — AI will foster the opportunity to give legal professionals back some of the time that has been squeezed from their days for far too long.
Time to be not only more productive but perhaps more time to be moms and dads, spouses, friends, and human beings in more meaningful ways.

kp.k: Leadership should combine experimentation with professional ethical foundations
kp.d: Smolik recommends that legal leaders actively lead with AI rather than simply adopt it. His proposed organizational culture encourages experimentation, curiosity and data-driven decisions while grounding adoption in ethics, judgment and integrity.
qs: As legal professionals, and particularly those of us in leadership positions, our role is not simply to adopt AI, but to lead with it.
That means creating a culture that encourages experimentation, data-driven decision-making, and curiosity about new ways of working.
It also means grounding the adoption of AI in ethics, judgment, and integrity — the timeless foundations of our profession.

kp.k: Future professional success pairs human judgment with AI capabilities
kp.d: Smolik predicts that legal professionals who embrace augmentation will thrive in a hypercompetitive industry. His professional ideal combines judgment, wisdom and experience with data, speed and efficiency; he expects this combination to improve advisory work and stewardship of financial resources.
qs: The lawyers and legal professionals who thrive in our hypercompetitive industry will be those who embrace augmentation — who see AI not as a threat or as competition, but as an opportunity to learn, improve and drive value.
The successful augmented legal professional will pair judgment with data, wisdom with speed, and experience with efficiency.

And just as every wave of technology before it, this one will make us more resilient, more efficient, better professionals and advisors… and, as importantly, better stewards of our financial resources.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Smolik predicts that AI will change how legal services are delivered, bought and sold by turning service information into data that strengthens corporate buyers' decisions.
pts.d: Mark A. Smolik, Chief Legal Officer of DHL Supply Chain Americas, argues that law departments will be able to automate invoice review, benchmark rates, analyze staffing patterns, evaluate workflows, and identify risks and opportunities. He predicts that legal services will evolve into a data-rich product, creating opportunities and shifting the buyer–seller relationship toward better-informed law departments. He does not specify a pricing model or quantify the anticipated shift.

pts.k: Smolik claims that AI already enables, and will further enable, cheaper, faster and better legal services through augmentation rather than replacement.
pts.d: He predicts productivity gains at individual, team and organizational levels through structured data, repetitive-task automation and ready access to information. He links these capabilities to additional capacity, better risk assessment and faster decisions. His framing retains legal professionals and combines their judgment and experience with AI-enabled information and efficiency.

pts.k: Smolik predicts that integrating AI into core legal-department processes can improve quality, enable anticipation of problems and reduce overall legal costs.
pts.d: The anticipated gains include less manual work, greater consistency in high-volume work, predictive analytics that support foresight, and decisions grounded in data rather than recalled experience. He also predicts competitive differentiation: professionals and departments that use data and AI effectively will create sustainable value, while those that do not will struggle under mounting cost pressure.

pts.k: Smolik predicts that AI could return time to legal professionals and improve work–life balance by taking on routine legal work.
pts.d: He identifies routine research, drafting and analysis as work AI can take on. The predicted benefit is an opportunity both for greater productivity and for more time with family and friends, rather than a guaranteed reduction in working hours.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on Smolik's professional experience, descriptions of current departmental activity, references to peer CLOs and historical analogy, rather than reported quantitative results.
pts.d: Smolik describes his DHL team's efforts to use AI to augment capacity and improve service delivery. He names CLOs at Duracell, Cargill, Mars Wrigley and Coherent as pursuing similar efforts with 'remarkable results,' but provides no concrete outcomes, methods or measurements. These are Smolik's reports, not independently presented claims from those CLOs. His non-replacement argument also draws an analogy with fax machines and email. The article supplies no datasets, model benchmarks, quantified cost or productivity gains, or detailed implementation cases. Eudia, Elevate, Epiq and PERSUIT are suggested as sources of guidance, not presented as measured evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Smolik presents augmentation as already underway as of 20 November 2025, with broader changes ahead but no dated forecast or adoption timetable.
pts.d: The article characterizes the present as an inflection point and describes some service improvements as already occurring. Most market, productivity and personal-time benefits are forward-looking. Conditions include effective AI use, structured data and integration into core processes. Maximizing the buyer's value also requires outside law firms to pursue lower total delivery costs. Smolik recommends experimentation, data-driven decision-making and ethical leadership as foundations for adoption, and acknowledges uncertainty about AI's impact and potential.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments as buyers, their outside law firms as providers, and lawyers and other legal professionals as workers.
pts.d: For corporate legal departments and their leaders, Smolik anticipates stronger purchasing decisions, more capacity, better risk and workflow analysis, and reduced total legal costs. Outside law firms are expected to adopt the same efficiency and cost objectives to maximize client value. Individual lawyers and other legal professionals are portrayed as augmented rather than displaced, with potential productivity and work–life benefits; those embracing augmentation are predicted to thrive competitively. The article does not offer distinct forecasts for junior lawyers, particular law-firm sizes, consumer legal services or access to justice.
